who-this-is-for.text: This page is for a reviewer who wants to play a naming claim instead of reading a walkthrough. The first-release naming profile is an explicit, labelled, unaccepted candidate, not the generic registry demo, and no on-chain acceptance is claimed. Open the simulator and choose the m1-naming profile.

what-you-can-do.text: Queue the first claim for the demo spelling alice: it waits while the key stays absent, because approval reserves nothing. Separately authorize withdrawal to copy the refund address stored in that request; redirection, Insert certification alone, cancellation after fold, and replay are refused. Then queue two claims for alice, fold the first to Active, and observe the competing fold refused with occupied-key. Resolve alice to read the certified fixture, and submit a crafted Delete to see naming-no-delete.

what-you-see-when-it-is-refused.text: Every refusal names its intended condition, and a generic exception is a defect. Cancellation refuses refund redirection, missing separate approval, an already folded claim, and replay. The remaining rows cover duplicate folding, crafted Delete, unapproved queueing, substituted representative identity, proposal misbinding, and unauthenticated resolution.

how-the-pieces-relate.text: The generic foundation of forty-one proved declarations stays upstream. The naming layer adds fixtures, queueing, folding, and observation with seventeen proved declarations of its own; the m1-naming engine transcribes that layer and never drives Lean from the browser. Choosing the profile is an explicit act: until m1-naming is selected its controls stay inert, and neither engine silently becomes the other.

what-is-proved-and-what-is-checked-here.text: Seventeen naming theorem declarations are proved in Lean from the standard axioms alone, separately from the generic forty-one. Seven record the user-facing claim contract; ten more pin transition, queue-validation, and resolution equations across the public boundary. The simulator replays a Lean-authored naming corpus of thirty-four rows and requires byte-identical verdicts, and the page's self-test replays the same corpus in the browser. Finite checks remain finite: they measure the transcription and prove nothing about acceptance.

fixture-fields-and-finite-model-limits.text: The playable claim card carries four fixture fields: an optional canonical payment destination, a canonical controller address, a thirty-two-byte next-control commitment, and a threshold quorum. The pending request also stores its refund address inside the Insert commitment, and cancellation can only copy it. No fee, deposit, price, bond, or refund-value schedule is invented. Retirement request withdrawal remains a distinct refusal case.

status-of-this-candidate.text: The claim, fold, and resolve naming profile is an unaccepted candidate: proven in Lean, replayed in the simulator, and playable in the browser. The Nix-built documentation archive packages its raw model, corpus, replay inputs, and exact identities for review. Building that bundle is not release publication or on-chain acceptance. The live preview is bound to the pull-request head and states that the candidate is unaccepted.

finding-alice.text: To find alice, take the registry's representative policy identifier and hash the spelling bytes with BLAKE2b two hundred and fifty-six, without a newline. The page shows the exact command also printed by register rows, plus a Koios query for the live UTxO. The holding address and datum distinguish an active record from retirement custody. If the UTxO result is empty, query the same asset's mint and burn history: minted once and burned once means permanent Over; never minted means unclaimed. This is the only place history is needed, and it is the asset's history, not the trie's.
